subtopics.title: Batch Job Overview
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how Mule 4 Batch Jobs process large record sets asynchronously and reliably, and when to use batch processing instead of a regular flow.
subtopics.summary: A Batch Job splits a large payload into individual records, processes them asynchronously through configurable steps, and reports success and failure per record.
subtopics.content_html:
Some integrations do not fit the typical request/response model. Migrating 50,000 customer records into Salesforce, reconciling a nightly file of transactions, or syncing a large product catalog all involve processing many individual records reliably, in parallel, with per-record error tracking. That is precisely the problem the Mule 4 Batch Job scope is designed to solve.

What a Batch Job Does

A Batch Job takes an incoming payload (typically a collection — an array, a list of database rows, lines from a file), splits it into individual records, and processes each record independently through one or more Batch Steps. Processing happens asynchronously in the background relative to the flow that triggered the job, and each record's success or failure is tracked individually, so one bad record does not stop the other 49,999 from processing.

Anatomy of a Batch Job

<flow name="import-customers-flow">
  <file:read path="customers.csv" />
  <ee:transform>
    <ee:message>
      <ee:set-payload><![CDATA[%dw 2.0
output application/java
---
payload]]></ee:set-payload>
    </ee:message>
  </ee:transform>

  <batch:job jobName="import-customers-batch">
    <batch:process-records>
      <batch:step name="validate-step">
        <choice>
          <when expression="#[payload.email == null]">
            <batch:record-variable
              variableName="isInvalid" value="true" />
          </when>
        </choice>
      </batch:step>

      <batch:step name="upsert-salesforce-step"
        acceptExpression="#[!vars.isInvalid]">
        <salesforce:upsert-object type="Contact"
          externalIdFieldName="Email__c" />
      </batch:step>
    </batch:process-records>

    <batch:on-complete>
      <logger message="Batch complete. Success: #[payload.successfulRecords], Failed: #[payload.failedRecords]" />
    </batch:on-complete>
  </batch:job>
</flow>

The Three Phases of a Batch Job

  1. Load and Dispatch (implicit) — the input payload is split into records and queued for processing. This happens automatically when the job starts.
  2. Process Records — each record moves through the sequence of Batch Steps you define, with each step running for every record (subject to any acceptExpression filtering).
  3. On Complete — a summary phase that runs once after all records finish processing, typically used for logging, sending a summary notification, or writing an audit record with counts of successful and failed records.

Asynchronous Execution

Because a Batch Job runs asynchronously, the flow that triggers it does not wait for all records to finish — control returns to the triggering flow almost immediately after the job is queued, and processing continues in the background using the runtime's batch thread pool. This makes Batch Jobs a natural fit behind a Scheduler or an HTTP endpoint that just needs to kick off a long-running import.

When to Use Batch Job vs a Regular Flow

ScenarioRecommended Approach
Processing a handful of records synchronously as part of a request/response APIRegular flow with a For Each or Parallel For Each
Processing thousands of records with per-record error isolation and reportingBatch Job
Long-running data migration or nightly reconciliationBatch Job, usually triggered by a Scheduler
Simple in-memory transformation with no per-item error tracking neededDataWeave / For Each

Record-Level Fault Tolerance

If a single record throws an unhandled error inside a Batch Step, that record is marked as failed and processing moves on to the next record — it does not abort the entire job. This is fundamentally different from a regular flow's default error-propagation behavior, and it is one of the main reasons teams choose Batch Job for large data sets: a handful of malformed records should not block the other 99% from completing.

Tip: Always inspect payload.failedRecords and the batch job's failure details in Runtime Manager after a run — silently ignoring per-record failures defeats much of the value of using Batch Job in the first place.

Key Points

  • Batch Job splits a large payload into individual records and processes each one through a sequence of Batch Steps.
  • Processing is asynchronous and record-level failures do not stop the overall job.
  • Every Batch Job has an implicit load/dispatch phase, one or more process-records steps, and an on-complete summary phase.
  • Use Batch Job for large-scale, fault-tolerant record processing; use simpler flow constructs for small, synchronous workloads.

subtopics.title: Batch Step and Aggregator
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how Batch Steps process individual records, how acceptExpression filters records, and how Batch Aggregator groups records for bulk operations.
subtopics.summary: Batch Steps process records one at a time inside a Batch Job, while the Batch Aggregator groups records into blocks for efficient bulk operations.
subtopics.content_html:
Inside a Batch Job, all the real processing logic lives in Batch Steps. Understanding how steps execute per record, how to filter which records a step applies to, and how the Batch Aggregator groups records for bulk operations is essential to building efficient, correct batch integrations.

Batch Steps Execute Per Record

Each <batch:step> you define inside <batch:process-records> runs once for every record in the job, in the order the steps are declared. A record moves through Step 1 for every record, then Step 2 for every record, and so on — not "all steps for record 1, then all steps for record 2." This matters when steps depend on record variables set by an earlier step.

<batch:process-records>
  <batch:step name="enrich-step">
    <http:request method="GET" path="/customers/#[payload.id]" config-ref="CRM_Config" />
    <batch:record-variable variableName="crmData" value="#[payload]" />
  </batch:step>

  <batch:step name="persist-step">
    <db:insert config-ref="Database_Config">
      <db:sql>INSERT INTO customers (id, name, crm_status) VALUES (:id, :name, :status)</db:sql>
      <db:input-parameters>#[{ id: payload.id, name: payload.name, status: vars.crmData.status }]</db:input-parameters>
    </db:insert>
  </batch:step>
</batch:process-records>

Filtering Records with acceptExpression

Not every step needs to run for every record. The acceptExpression attribute lets a step opt out of records that do not meet a condition, based on the record's payload or any record variables set by a previous step.

<batch:step name="send-welcome-email-step"
  acceptExpression="#[vars.isNewCustomer == true]">
  <email:send config-ref="SMTP_Config" subject="Welcome!" />
</batch:step>

Records that do not satisfy the expression simply skip that step and move to the next one; they are not marked as failed.

Filtering by Record Status with acceptPolicy

The acceptPolicy attribute controls whether a step should process records that already failed in an earlier step: ALL_RECORDS processes every record regardless of prior failures, while ONLY_FAILURES (or the equivalent successful-only setting) restricts the step to records already in a particular state. This lets you build steps dedicated to handling or logging failures separately from the main happy path.

The Batch Aggregator

Many downstream systems (Salesforce bulk APIs, batch database inserts, file writes) are far more efficient when you send them a block of records at once instead of one call per record. The Batch Aggregator, configured inside a batch step with the <batch:aggregator> element, groups records into blocks of a configurable size and lets you process each block together.

<batch:step name="bulk-upsert-step">
  <batch:aggregator size="200">
    <salesforce:upsert-bulk type="Contact" externalIdFieldName="Email__c">
      <salesforce:records>#[payload]</salesforce:records>
    </salesforce:upsert-bulk>
  </batch:aggregator>
</batch:step>

Inside the aggregator, payload is no longer a single record — it is a list of up to size records collected together, ready to be sent to an API or database that supports bulk operations.

Why Aggregation Matters for Performance

ApproachAPI/DB Calls for 10,000 Records
One record per call10,000 calls
Aggregated in blocks of 20050 calls

Reducing round trips this dramatically often means the difference between a batch job finishing in minutes versus hours, and it significantly reduces load on rate-limited external APIs like the Salesforce Bulk API.

Tip: Choose an aggregator size that matches the target system's recommended bulk batch size — Salesforce Bulk API, for instance, has documented optimal batch sizes that are worth checking rather than guessing.

Key Points

  • Batch Steps run per record, in declared order, across the entire record set before moving to the next step.
  • acceptExpression filters which records a given step processes; acceptPolicy filters based on prior success/failure status.
  • The Batch Aggregator groups records into configurable-size blocks for efficient bulk operations.
  • Aggregating records dramatically reduces the number of downstream API/database calls for large data sets.

subtopics.title: Scheduler in Mule
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how the Mule 4 Scheduler source triggers flows on fixed frequency or cron-based schedules, and best practices for scheduled flow design.
subtopics.summary: The Scheduler is a Mule 4 flow source that triggers a flow automatically on a fixed interval or a cron expression, without any external trigger.
subtopics.content_html:
Many integrations do not start with an inbound HTTP request or a message on a queue — they need to run on their own, on a timer: pull a file every night, poll a database every five minutes, or kick off a batch reconciliation every Monday morning. The Scheduler source is the Mule 4 building block for exactly that.

What the Scheduler Does

The Scheduler is a flow source (it goes at the very start of a flow, just like an HTTP Listener) that triggers the flow automatically according to a configured schedule, with no external caller involved. Every time the schedule fires, a brand-new Mule event is created and the flow executes from the top.

Fixed Frequency Scheduling

The simplest scheduling strategy runs the flow repeatedly at a fixed time interval.

<flow name="nightly-file-import-flow">
  <scheduler>
    <scheduling-strategy>
      <fixed-frequency frequency="15" timeUnit="MINUTES" />
    </scheduling-strategy>
  </scheduler>

  <sftp:read path="/incoming/orders.csv" config-ref="SFTP_Config" />
  <flow-ref name="process-orders-subflow" />
</flow>

This flow runs every 15 minutes, starting as soon as the application deploys. Fixed frequency also supports a startDelay attribute to offset the very first execution.

Cron-Based Scheduling

For anything more specific than "every N minutes" — like "every weekday at 6 AM" or "on the first day of the month" — use a cron expression instead.

<flow name="monthly-reconciliation-flow">
  <scheduler>
    <scheduling-strategy>
      <cron expression="0 0 6 1 * ?" timeZone="America/New_York" />
    </scheduling-strategy>
  </scheduler>

  <flow-ref name="reconciliation-batch-subflow" />
</flow>

That expression fires at 6:00 AM Eastern Time on the first day of every month. Always set an explicit timeZone; relying on the server's default time zone is a common source of scheduling bugs when applications move between regions or CloudHub workers.

Preventing Overlapping Runs

If a scheduled flow takes longer to run than the interval between executions (for example, a 20-minute import scheduled every 15 minutes), you can end up with overlapping executions competing for the same resources. Common mitigations include:

  • Using an Object Store-backed lock at the start of the flow to prevent a new run from starting while a previous run is still in progress.
  • Widening the schedule interval to comfortably exceed the expected processing time.
  • Delegating the heavy lifting to a Batch Job, which is designed for exactly this kind of long-running, asynchronous work.

Scheduler Behavior on CloudHub with Multiple Workers

When an application with a Scheduler is deployed to CloudHub with more than one worker, by default every worker runs its own copy of the schedule, which usually is not what you want (e.g., importing the same file three times). Enable the Object Store-based clustering behavior or the primary node only setting available in Runtime Manager so the scheduled flow only executes on one worker at a time.

Tip: In Runtime Manager, look for the "Run on primary node only" clustering option when deploying a multi-worker application that contains a Scheduler — skipping this is a very common source of duplicated scheduled processing in production.

Scheduler vs Poll Scope

AspectSchedulerPoll Scope
PurposeTrigger a flow on a timer, regardless of data stateRepeatedly check a source for new/changed data and only proceed when something is found
Built-in change detectionNoYes, via watermarking
Typical useKick off a batch job, run a report, trigger housekeeping tasksDetect new database rows, new files, new messages since last check

Key Points

  • The Scheduler source triggers a flow automatically on a fixed frequency or a cron expression.
  • Always set an explicit time zone on cron schedules to avoid environment-dependent bugs.
  • Guard against overlapping executions when a run can take longer than the schedule interval.
  • On multi-worker CloudHub deployments, restrict scheduled execution to a single node to avoid duplicate processing.

subtopics.title: Poll Scope
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how the Poll scope repeatedly checks a source for new data, how watermarking avoids reprocessing, and common Poll scope patterns.
subtopics.summary: The Poll scope repeatedly executes a source operation on a schedule and uses watermarking to detect and process only new or changed data.
subtopics.content_html:
Plenty of systems you integrate with have no way to push events to you — no webhook, no message queue, nothing. A legacy database table, a directory that occasionally receives new files, or a SaaS API with only a "list records" endpoint all require you to go check periodically for anything new. The Mule 4 Poll scope is purpose-built for this "check periodically and only act on what's new" pattern.

What Poll Does

The Poll scope wraps a single operation (a database query, an HTTP request, a file listing, etc.) and runs it on a schedule, exactly like the Scheduler source. What makes Poll different is built-in support for watermarking: remembering, between executions, the last value seen (such as a timestamp or an ID), so each run can filter for only records newer than that watermark.

Basic Poll Structure

<flow name="poll-new-orders-flow">
  <poll>
    <scheduling-strategy>
      <fixed-frequency frequency="5" timeUnit="MINUTES" />
    </scheduling-strategy>

    <db:select config-ref="Database_Config">
      <db:sql>
        SELECT * FROM orders WHERE updated_at > :lastWatermark ORDER BY updated_at ASC
      </db:sql>
      <db:input-parameters>#[{ lastWatermark: Mule::p('poll.watermark.default') }]</db:input-parameters>
    </db:select>

    <poll:watermark
      variable="lastWatermark"
      selector="MAX"
      selectorExpression="#[payload[-1].updated_at]" />
  </poll>

  <foreach>
    <flow-ref name="process-order-subflow" />
  </foreach>
</flow>

How Watermarking Works

  1. On the first execution, there is no stored watermark, so the query typically uses a default starting value (e.g., epoch 0 or the current date).
  2. The wrapped operation runs and returns a set of records.
  3. The <poll:watermark> element inspects the result (via selectorExpression) and computes a new watermark value (via selector, e.g., MAX or MIN).
  4. The new watermark is persisted, by default in the application's Object Store, so it survives across polling cycles and even application restarts.
  5. On the next execution, the stored watermark is available as a variable and used to filter the query so only new/changed records come back.

Avoiding Empty-Result Waste

By default, if a poll execution returns no records (nothing new since the last watermark), Mule does not push an empty payload through the rest of the flow — the flow's downstream processors simply do not execute for that cycle. This means you do not need to manually guard against empty result sets after every poll.

Poll with Idempotent Message Validation

Watermarking reduces duplicate processing but is not always perfectly precise (for example, multiple records sharing the exact same timestamp at a boundary). For stronger guarantees, combine Poll with an Idempotent Message Validator, which tracks already-processed record IDs in an Object Store and filters out true duplicates even if the same record is returned by two consecutive poll executions.

<idempotent-message-validator idExpression="#[payload.orderId]" valueExpression="#[payload.updated_at]" />

Poll vs Scheduler

AspectPollScheduler
Wraps an operation with change detectionYes (watermarking)No
Skips downstream processing on no new dataYes, automaticallyNo, always runs the flow
Typical useDetecting new/changed records from a source with no native change feedTime-based triggers unrelated to data state (e.g., nightly report generation)

Common Poll Use Cases

  • Polling a database table for newly inserted or updated rows.
  • Checking an SFTP directory for new files since the last check.
  • Calling a SaaS REST API's "list changed records since" endpoint on a schedule.
Tip: Always choose a watermark column that is monotonically increasing and reliably updated (like an auto-incrementing ID or a properly maintained updated_at timestamp) — a poorly chosen watermark field is the most common cause of missed or duplicated records in polling integrations.

Key Points

  • Poll wraps a single operation and runs it on a schedule, adding built-in watermarking for change detection.
  • The watermark is persisted in Object Store and used to filter each subsequent execution to only new/changed data.
  • Poll automatically skips downstream processing when a cycle returns no new records.
  • Pair Poll with an Idempotent Message Validator for stronger duplicate protection at record boundaries.
